title: Legally enforceable debt under NI Act when loan violates Section 269SS
description: The Kerala High Court held that the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt, but the accused may rebut this presumption on the standard of preponderance of probabilities. Where the complainant admits that the alleged loan exceeding ₹20,000 was paid in cash in violation of Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act, such a transaction may not constitute a legally enforceable debt unless a valid explanation under Section 273B is shown. Courts cannot enforce transactions that defeat the statutory objective of preventing unaccounted cash dealings. Consequently, the presumption under Section 139 was successfully rebutted and the conviction under Section 138 NI Act was set aside.

title: CCI jurisdiction despite sectoral telecom regulation
description: The Kerala High Court held that the Competition Commission of India retains jurisdiction to investigate abuse of dominant position under the Competition Act, 2002 even when the relevant sector is regulated by another statutory authority such as the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI). The existence of sector-specific regulation does not exclude the application of competition law where anti-competitive conduct is alleged. The Court further held that an order under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act directing investigation is only a prima facie administrative determination and does not decide rights or impose civil consequences. Therefore, judicial interference through writ jurisdiction at this preliminary stage is generally unwarranted.

title: Applicability of Shops and Establishments Act to IT companies
description: The Kerala High Court held that IT and IT-enabled service companies operating in the state fall within the definition of commercial establishments under the Kerala Shops and Commercial Establishments Act unless a specific statutory exemption is granted. The nature of business as a technology or software enterprise does not automatically remove such establishments from the regulatory framework of labour legislation. Labour authorities are therefore empowered to conduct inspections and initiate proceedings to ensure compliance with statutory requirements under the Act. Courts should not interfere with such inspections where authorities act within the scope of their statutory powers.

title: Doctrine of merger after dismissal of Special Leave Petition
description: The Supreme Court clarified the doctrine of merger in the context of dismissal of Special Leave Petitions under Article 136 of the Constitution. The Court held that dismissal of an SLP at the stage of consideration for grant of leave does not result in merger of the High Court judgment into the order of the Supreme Court. At that stage the Court exercises discretionary jurisdiction and not appellate jurisdiction. A non-speaking dismissal merely indicates that the Court was not inclined to grant leave and does not constitute affirmation of the High Court judgment. Consequently, the High Court retains jurisdiction to entertain review proceedings against its own judgment, subject to procedural limitations.

title: Distinction between murder and culpable homicide
description: The Supreme Court examined the distinction between murder under Section 302 IPC and culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 IPC. The Court held that determining the appropriate offence requires careful evaluation of intention, knowledge, nature of the weapon used, the number and location of injuries, and surrounding circumstances. Where the accused intentionally inflicts multiple injuries on vital parts of the body using a deadly weapon, intention to cause death may be inferred. In the present case, eyewitness testimony corroborated by medical evidence established the accused’s intention to cause death, and therefore the conviction under Section 302 IPC was upheld.

title: Limitation and readiness in suits for specific performance
description: The Supreme Court reiterated that a decree for specific performance requires the plaintiff to demonstrate continuous readiness and willingness to perform contractual obligations under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act. The Court held that reliance on contractual extensions granted by a person lacking valid authority cannot establish enforceable rights against a co-owner who had revoked earlier authority through a registered power of attorney. The Court further clarified that under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, a suit for specific performance must be filed within three years from the date fixed for performance or from the date when the plaintiff has notice of refusal. In the absence of a valid extension binding on the relevant party, the suit filed beyond the limitation period was barred.

title: Procedural order granting time for filing rejoinder
description: The Supreme Court issued an interim procedural order granting the respondent additional time to file a rejoinder affidavit in a pending Special Leave Petition. The matter was directed to be listed again after the specified period. Such orders do not decide substantive legal rights or interpret statutory provisions but are issued to facilitate orderly progress of proceedings before the Court.

title: Reservation in promotion for persons with disabilities
description: The Supreme Court held that the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995 mandates reservation in promotion in addition to reservation in initial recruitment. Sections 32, 33 and 47 must be read harmoniously to ensure equal opportunity and non-discrimination in employment for persons with disabilities. The Court clarified that reservation must be computed with reference to total cadre strength and is not confined to employees originally appointed under the disability quota. Once an employee qualifies as a person with disability under the statute, the benefit of reservation in promotion applies irrespective of the mode of initial recruitment.

title: DNA evidence and commutation of death sentence in rape-murder case
description: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of the accused for rape and murder of a minor child based on a complete chain of circumstantial evidence supported by forensic and DNA analysis. The Court reiterated that in cases relying on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a chain of circumstances that conclusively points to the guilt of the accused and excludes any reasonable alternative hypothesis. In the present case, the forensic reports, medical findings, and recovery evidence decisively connected the accused to the offence. However, the Court held that the imposition of the death penalty requires strict application of the 'rarest of rare' doctrine, balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Despite the gravity of the crime, the Court found that the mitigating factors and possibility of reformation justified commutation of the death sentence to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused’s natural life.

title: Legislative competence to impose building tax
description: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975, holding that the State Legislature possessed competence under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to impose taxes on buildings. The Court clarified the distinction between the subject of a tax and the measure used to compute it, observing that determining capital value by multiplying annual rental value was a permissible method of valuation. The retrospective operation of the tax from an earlier date was also upheld, as it did not violate constitutional protections or impair vested rights. The Court rejected the challenge under Article 14, finding the valuation mechanism reasonable and non-arbitrary.
statutes: Constitution of India Entry 49 List II

title: Basic structure doctrine of the Constitution
description: The Supreme Court in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case held that while Parliament has wide powers to amend the Constitution under Article 368, such power is not unlimited. Parliament cannot alter or destroy the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution. The Court identified foundational principles such as supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and judicial review as part of the Constitution’s basic structure. While the 24th Amendment confirming Parliament’s amending power was upheld, parts of the 25th Amendment were limited, and laws placed in the Ninth Schedule remain subject to judicial review if they damage the basic structure.
